episode_title: Tom Panos: How to Know When the Australian Property Market Has Hit the Bottom

real_qa.q: What are the key indicators to identify when the Australian property market has hit bottom?
real_qa.r: Tom Panos identifies six main indicators: clearance rates showing improvement over a six-week period consistently; increasing numbers at open for inspections; growth in registered bidders at auctions; days on market stopping growth and potentially shortening; and nice homes being quickly snapped up, signaling sentiment change. He emphasizes looking at patterns rather than single-week data, and notes that Sydney and Melbourne will likely come out of the correction first, followed by other markets.

real_qa.q: Why has the Australian Labor government budget failed to address the housing supply crisis?
real_qa.r: Tom Panos states the Labor government has not addressed the supply issue, meaning Australia will be years behind on housing supply. Builders and developers have stopped building because construction costs are too high and replacement values don't justify development margins—the numbers don't stack up. Without supply growth, prices will continue rising once the market recovers, creating an unintended consequence where first-home buyer measures failed despite being the stated goal.
real_qa.requete: Labor government housing supply crisis Australia

real_qa.q: How should property investors respond to the current Australian property market correction?
real_qa.r: Rather than trying to catch the bottom of the market, Tom Panos recommends buying well: purchasing A-grade properties in A-grade locations with reasonable income certainty and a holding period of at least two to three years. He emphasizes this is not about timing the absolute bottom, but getting good value now compared to six to nine months ago. Current conditions offer better yields, less competition from other buyers, and more stock availability for investors with capital.

real_qa.q: What did Tom Panos's coaching group of 88 property professionals discover about business opportunity during market downturns?
real_qa.r: Tom's black belt coaching group, consisting of 88 professionals each generating $2 million-plus annually, found that market volume dropped roughly 30%, leaving 70% of business available. Every member agreed they could maintain a good income and lifestyle on 70% of business by working harder, being longer, and picking up market share from competitors leaving the industry. This demonstrated that downturns present opportunities for disciplined businesses to consolidate market position.

real_qa.q: Why do first-home buyers in Australia face negative equity risk from recent government budget changes?
real_qa.r: First-home buyer lending decreased by 20% following the budget. Many first-time buyers were attracted with 5% deposits to purchase $1 million properties, borrowing $950,000. When property values dropped to $800,000, these buyers lost their deposit money while still owing the full $950,000 borrowed, creating negative equity. This occurred despite the budget being positioned as helping first-home buyers, making them among the policy's main casualties.
real_qa.requete: first-home buyers negative equity Australia budget

guest.titre: Real Estate Investment Expert and Property Market Commentator
guest.bio_context: Tom Panos is a real estate professional with over 40 years of experience who has lived through seven major property market corrections, including the 1990-1993 Paul Keating recession, the GFC, and the Royal Commission period. He previously worked under Rupert Murdoch and has built a significant media presence through his Sunday Night Rant series and podcast appearances, becoming a recognized voice on Australian property market sentiment and investment strategy.
